transfers.label: 1547 lease
transfers.instrument: A 1,000-year lease of Cydwin (the Great House) from Sir George Herbert to Vaughan. The lease itself is not in hand.
transfers.note: Sir George Herbert held the manor of Llandough by 1545 (rent-roll in Cardiff Records). The Vaughans, a minor gentry family, held the Great House, the chief freehold farm of the parish, from the mid-16th century to the later 18th (Heneb HER). Historical family only. A present-day family of the same name has told us it is not related.

transfers.label: 1767 marriage
transfers.instrument: Inheritance by marriage: William Hurst and Calvert Richard Jones had married two heiresses of this branch of the Herbert family, and by 1767 held the manors of Dinas Powys, Llandough East and Cogan.
transfers.note: Cardiff Records: from 1545 the manor passed from Sir George Herbert to his grandson Sir William Herbert, and stayed with the Herberts of Cogan Pill for several generations.

root.name: Root title chain
root.intro: Freehold title path and evidential gaps. The separate three-arrow diagram shows the later synthetic A1–A3 registration endpoints; those arrows are a pattern under examination, not freehold conveyances. Solid lines mark a recorded title-level step; dashed lines mark a missing instrument or a link supported by secondary material or a family statement.

steps.label: Vaughan freehold evidenced from the mid-16th century
steps.text: Heneb's HER records the Vaughans holding the Great House—the parish's chief freehold farm—from the mid-16th century to the later 18th. A 1547, 1,000-year lease from Sir George Herbert to Vaughan is also recorded in the research note, but that lease is not itself proof of the freehold conveyance; the instrument is not in hand. The diagram treats the Vaughan freehold as supported by historical evidence, not as a fully inspected conveyance.

steps.note: Historical freehold tenure is recorded by Heneb; the cited 1547 lease is not a freehold conveyance instrument.

steps.label: Vaughan → Bute Estate · freehold, early 19th century
steps.text: Heneb's HER records the Bute Estate holding the Great House freehold in the early 19th century, with the manorial courts for Llandough and Leckwith held in the house. The conveyance, its exact date and the vendor are not located: this link is an explicit evidential gap. The manorial lordship reached Bute separately (Herbert → Hurst & Jones by 1767 → Bute in 1793); that is not treated as the house-farm freehold transfer.

src.t: Heneb HER GGAT02038s · Great House Farm (Vaughan freehold; Bute in the early 19th century)
EV-0003 · Bute Estate records 1552–1824 naming Cydfin / Ty Mawr Farm (Evidence Register)

steps.label: 1877 split · Parcel A to Daniel Thomas & Son
steps.text: The working title-chain hypothesis is that the Bute Estate parted with the farmhouse, buildings and about 10 acres (Parcel A) to Daniel Thomas & Son in 1877, while retaining about 9 acres (Parcel B). The agreement is not in hand, so the precise legal instrument and whether it was a freehold sale or quarry arrangement remain unresolved. The cited family statement and NLW catalogue are supporting sources, not a substitute for the deed.

src.t: EV-0291 · NLW Bute Estate catalogue D153 (Llandough limeworks land, 1876–1912)
Legal Wiki · Three parts of Parcel A (page 3356)

steps.label: 1877 split · Parcel B kept by the Bute Estate, then Mountjoy Ltd (1926)
steps.text: In 1877 the Bute Estate keeps about 9 acres “up on the top” (Parcel B; Timeline page 33). The Bute Estate still holds it in 1916 (EV-0014). In 1926 the remaining Bute property is incorporated as Mountjoy Ltd (Glamorgan Archives DA catalogue). The records place Mountjoy in 1926, not 1877.

src.t: EV-0014 · 1916 Bute yearly tenancy, with plan
Glamorgan Archives DA catalogue (Bute estate history)

steps.label: Parcel B · Mountjoy / Bute → Western Ground Rents
steps.text: Conveyance on sale, Mountjoy / Bute to Western Ground Rents Ltd, 25 Dec 1938 (recited in later WGR deeds). The deed and its plan are not held, so exactly which land it carried is still open. A 1939 tenancy plan shows WGR letting Parcel B only.

src.t: EV-0216 · recital of the conveyance of 25 Dec 1938

steps.label: Parcel B · Western Ground Rents → BP Pension Trust
steps.text: Conveyance, WGR to BP Pension Trust, recited as the root of BP’s title. For the house it carried the benefit of the 1962 order. BP’s agreed bid of 15 Feb 1969 took WGR’s properties “for their pension fund” (press). In September 1974 BP applied for leave to enforce the 1962 order. The conveyance and plan are not held.

src.t: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2 (judgment)

EV-0288 · 1968–69 press on the WGR takeover

steps.title: WA231076
steps.label: Parcel B · BP Properties registers WA231076
steps.text: BP Properties Ltd applies to register title WA231076 (the farm). The application date is in HM Land Registry’s file schedule. The transfer from BP Pension Trust to BP Properties is not held.

steps.label: Parcel A · Williams family (1928 on the family's case)
steps.text: Quarrying ended and the last rent of about £4 was paid to Alfred Thomas, son of Daniel Thomas. On the family's case, Parcel A then passed to the Williams family under the 1877 arrangement. The 1928 receipt and Mary (Nancy) Williams's statement are the cited sources; no conveyance deed has been located.

steps.label: Parcel A · no later freehold conveyance located
steps.text: On the documents presently identified, the freehold chain for Parcel A stops with the Williams family after 1928. No later deed has been located conveying Parcel A, or its parts A1, A2 or A3, from Williams to WGR, BP or a current possessor. The later possession orders, licence letters, deeds and registrations are separately displayed below as record chronologies; they are not shown as conveyances from Williams.

src.t: Legal Wiki · Three parts of Parcel A

paths.intro: Pick a part of Parcel A (A1, A2, A3) or Parcel B to light only its path. 💩 marks a permissive-occupancy step, 💩💩 a seizure or possession step. Each year sits where the line arrives.

question.title: The question
question.text: How did the family, holders of Parcel A on the root title chain, come to be treated as permissive occupiers by the three parties that each registered a part of it (A1 the woodland, A2 the house and yard, A3 the green)?

src.t: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2 (judgment)

lines.title: A3 · 1959 permissive occupancy attempt (refused)
lines.text: Mary refused an offer to let her the occupied farmhouse, buildings and garden in 1959 and asserted ownership through her grandfather. The family records this as the step that started the 12 years for the green. The 1987 judgment ties the offer to the farmhouse and garden. Source to add: the 1959 offer and reply, and any 1958 record.

lines.title: A3 · 1970 village-green registration VG41
lines.text: VG41 was registered on 16 June 1970 by Glamorgan County Council as registration authority. The original VG41 file (application, map, ownership section, notices and any decision) is outstanding. Registration alone did not vest the green in the authority or prove who owned the freehold.

lines.title: A3 · Llandough Community Council today
lines.text: Llandough Community Council states that it owns and maintains the village green. How the green came to it is not established: in 1970 Llandough lay in Penarth Urban District, and the Community Council was formed in 1982.

lines.text: The 1955 possession order was framed for the “whole farm”. On 4 July 1955 possession was taken of every part of the farm except the farmhouse and garden. Its schedule and plan are not held, so which Parcel-A ground it reached is unclear.

lines.text: Cardiff County Court possession order against Frederick and Mary for the farmhouse, buildings and garden. It was never enforced. The family’s case is that it could not lawfully be enforced later. The order itself is not yet held (EV-0041 pending).

lines.text: The warrant was withdrawn and BP’s licence letters were sent the same day, offering Mrs Buckler the house and garden rent free for life. She did not accept them. The 1987 judgment treated the letters as a licence, so her possession after that date was not counted towards the 12 years.

lines.title: 1974 · BP fail to extinguish
lines.date: Sep 1974 (leave to enforce sought) · 31 Oct 1974 (warrant withdrawn)
lines.text: In September 1974 BP applied for leave to enforce the 1962 order against the house. On 31 October 1974 the warrant was withdrawn and licence letters were sent instead. The order was not carried out, and the family stayed in the house.
